newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Littlewoods to sell trademark stores.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Littlewoods to sell trademark stores.

text.p: Britain's largest private company Littlewoods said on Tuesday said it was putting its poorly performing chain of 135 town centre shops up for sale in a major shake-up, which could put a question mark over thousands of jobs.

The retailer, whose trademark Littlewoods stores have become a household name since the first one opened in Blackpool in 1937, wants to sell the shops to focus on its mail order and leisure businesses, which include football pools.

The sale of the stores, estimated to be worth more than 500 million pounds ($800 million), would represent a key step in the overhaul of the leisure and retailing group since James Ross, former chief executive of Cable and Wireless Plc, took over as chairman last year.
Ross said Littlewoods had already had approaches from potential buyers and would soon have a short list of purchasers, but he stressed the sale would only go ahead at the right price.
"We've had people sniffing around as it were over the last few months," Ross said in a telephone interview.
He said Littlewoods wanted to sell the stores, which employ 10,000 staff, as a going concern. Ross said food retailers could be among those interested in buying the shops.

"We think there are about half a dozen (retailers) who have the capability of paying a really interesting price," Ross said, but declined to give a figure. Ross said the group hoped to decide whether to proceed with a sale by the summer.

The shopworkers union Usdaw expressed anger at the announcement to the press before staff were consulted. Spokesman Michael Gordon said in a statement, " I shall be seeking a firm commitment from Littlewoods...that any prospective buyer will guarantee continuity of employment and pension rights for our members."

The Moores family, which owns the group, has reportedly been dissatisfied with the company's recent performance and came close to selling the whole business in 1995. But Ross said that a sale of the entire group was not now on the agenda.

But he said Littlewoods considered it was a good time to sell the stores, a move which might deliver better value to shareholders. A booming retail market, rising rents and restriction on out-of-town developments could make the group's stores attractive.
"There are a number of people hungry for extra space...If they can do better off the square footage than we can you might just find...quite a lot of interest coming through."

The sale would leave Littlewoods with home shopping and betting on football pools. The group, number two in Britain in home shopping after market leader Great Universal Stores Plc is trying to expand home shopping via the purchase of Freemans mail order from retailer Sears Plc. The 390 million pound deal is contingent on approval by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
Littlewoods reported a 15 percent rise in overall profits for 1996 to 211.1 million pounds ($340.8 million) before tax, with sales down slightly to 2.28 billion.

Home shopping sales rose last year by about seven percent, with the agency business achieving an eight percent increase in sales per agent. The group's Index Extra direct mail order catalogue - launched nationally in July 1996 - saw sales rise to 116 million pounds from about 32 million. Ross said the direct mail side was "steaming away," but the old-style agency operation was still profitable and would be around for a long time.
Trading profit from mail order was up about 50 percent to 55 million stg from 36.7 million.
Ross said Littlewoods' football pools business was still being hit by competition from Britain's National Lottery, especially since last month's launch of a midweek lottery.
"How much we can't really say because we don't think that has settled down to any pattern yet." He said it would take two or three months at least before the full impact became apparent.

He said Littlewoods was trying to differentiate the pools from the lottery and was striving to cut costs to try and soften the blow of lower sales, which fell last year to 459 million pounds from 631 million. Operating profit fell less than five percent to 22.8 million pounds.

Ross said that as the midweek lottery took a bigger share of customer spending, it was inevitable the group would have to look for further efficiencies, which had in the past resulted in redundancies. ($ = 0.619 British Pounds)
